topics.title: Tenses
topics.summary: How to choose the right present, past and future forms to show when an action happens and how it relates to other actions.

rules.rule: Use the simple present for habits, general truths and fixed timetables.
examples: The cabinet meets every Tuesday.
Ice floats on water.

rules.rule: Use the present continuous for actions in progress now or for temporary situations. Stative verbs such as know, believe, own and prefer do not normally take the continuous form.
examples: The students are revising for their finals this week.
I believe him. (not: I am believing him.)

rules.rule: Use the present perfect to link a past action to the present. Do not use it with a finished time expression such as yesterday, last year, in 2019 or ago.
examples: The Senate has passed the bill.
The Senate passed the bill last week.

rules.rule: Use the present perfect continuous with for or since to show an activity that began in the past and is still continuing.
examples: She has been teaching at the college since 2016.
We have been waiting for forty minutes.

rules.rule: Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
examples: The guests had left before the power returned.
He realised that he had forgotten his admit card.

rules.rule: In time and condition clauses introduced by when, if, until, before, after or as soon as, use a present tense for future meaning, not will.
examples: I will call you when I reach Multan.
If the weather clears, the flight will depart on time.

rules.rule: Use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a particular future time.
examples: At this time tomorrow, we will be sitting the essay paper.
She will be travelling to Gilgit next weekend.

questions.prompt: Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
questions.explanation: This is a general scientific truth, so the simple present (boils) is required.

questions.prompt: I ___ this novel since Monday, and I am only halfway through.
questions.explanation: An activity that started in the past (since Monday) and is still continuing takes the present perfect continuous; 'am reading since' is incorrect.

questions.prompt: By the time the inspector arrived, the clerks ___ the files.
questions.explanation: The shredding happened before another past action (the inspector arrived), so the past perfect is needed.

questions.prompt: The minister ___ the province last year.
questions.explanation: 'Last year' is a finished time expression, so the simple past is required; the present perfect cannot be used with it.

questions.prompt: Please wait here until the director ___.
questions.explanation: In a time clause beginning with 'until', a present tense is used for future meaning, not will or going to.

questions.prompt: She ___ the answer, but she will not tell us.
questions.explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms, so the simple present 'knows' is correct.

questions.prompt: When we reached the hall, the lecture ___, so we missed the opening remarks.
questions.explanation: The lecture began before we reached the hall (both in the past), so the earlier action takes the past perfect.

questions.prompt: Listen! Someone ___ at the door.
questions.explanation: 'Listen!' shows the action is happening at this moment, so the present continuous is needed.

questions.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
questions.explanation: In a first conditional, the if-clause takes the simple present even though it refers to the future.

questions.prompt: He ___ in Lahore for ten years before he moved to Karachi in 2015.
questions.explanation: The period in Lahore came before another past event (moving in 2015), so the past perfect is correct; present perfect forms cannot refer to a finished past period.

questions.prompt: This time next year, I ___ for my CSS interview.
questions.explanation: An action that will be in progress at a specific future time ('this time next year') takes the future continuous.

questions.prompt: It is the first time I ___ such a well-argued essay.
questions.explanation: After 'It is the first time', standard English uses the present perfect (have read).

questions.prompt: Every morning my grandfather ___ a walk in Lawrence Garden.
questions.explanation: A daily habit takes the simple present (takes); 'is taking' describes an action in progress, not a routine.

questions.prompt: Look! The children ___ in the rain.
questions.explanation: 'Look!' signals an action happening now, so the present continuous is needed; the simple present 'play' expresses habit.

questions.prompt: The Sun ___ in the east.
questions.explanation: Permanent facts take the simple present; the continuous 'is rising' suggests a temporary action.

questions.prompt: I ___ what you mean now; thank you for explaining.
questions.explanation: 'Understand' is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms, so the simple present is correct.

questions.prompt: This parcel ___ to my brother, so please do not open it.
questions.explanation: 'Belong' is stative and takes the simple present; 'belong' is wrong because the singular subject needs -s.

questions.prompt: We ___ Murree three times so far this year.
questions.explanation: 'So far this year' links the past to the present, so the present perfect is required; the simple past suits a finished period.

questions.prompt: The Quaid-e-Azam ___ in 1948.
questions.explanation: A finished event at a stated past time takes the simple past; the present perfect cannot be used with a definite past date.

questions.prompt: I ___ the report when the electricity went off.
questions.explanation: A longer action interrupted by a shorter past event takes the past continuous; present forms clash with 'went off'.

questions.prompt: She ___ three books since she retired.
questions.explanation: 'Since' with a period lasting until now requires the present perfect; the simple past 'wrote' cannot combine with 'since' here.

questions.prompt: By the end of this month, the committee ___ its report.
questions.explanation: 'By' + a future time calls for the future perfect, showing completion before that point; 'has submitted' refers to the present.

questions.prompt: The Karachi express ___ at 6.45 tomorrow morning, so do not be late.
questions.explanation: Timetabled future events take the simple present; past and perfect forms contradict 'tomorrow'.

questions.prompt: I ___ to Quetta next Friday; I have already bought my ticket.
questions.explanation: A fixed personal arrangement for the future uses the present continuous; past forms clash with 'next Friday'.

questions.prompt: They ___ for the bus for forty minutes when it finally arrived.
questions.explanation: An action continuing up to a past moment takes the past perfect continuous; 'have been waiting' reaches only to the present.

questions.prompt: When you arrive at the airport tomorrow, my cousin ___ for you at the gate.
questions.explanation: An action in progress at a future moment takes the future continuous; 'waits' does not express a future action in progress.

questions.prompt: By 2030, engineers ___ on the dam for twelve years.
questions.explanation: Duration up to a future point takes the future perfect continuous; 'had been working' looks back from the past, not the future.

questions.prompt: He told me yesterday that he ___ the letter the previous week.
questions.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, an earlier past action shifts to the past perfect; 'has posted' breaks the sequence of tenses.

questions.prompt: Our teacher explained that light ___ faster than sound.
questions.explanation: A universal truth keeps the simple present even after a past reporting verb; the past perfect wrongly suggests a finished past event.

questions.prompt: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation: The second conditional uses the past subjunctive 'were' for unreal present situations; 'am' belongs to real conditions.

questions.prompt: If she had studied harder, she ___ the exam.
questions.explanation: The third conditional pairs 'had + past participle' with 'would have + past participle'; 'will pass' belongs to the first conditional.

questions.prompt: As soon as the results ___, I will inform you.
questions.explanation: In time clauses about the future, English uses a present tense, not 'will'; so 'are announced' is correct.

questions.prompt: I will ring you after I ___ the meeting.
questions.explanation: A time clause introduced by 'after' takes a present tense for future reference; 'will finish' is not used in such clauses.

questions.prompt: She ___ her keys, so she cannot get into the house.
questions.explanation: A past action with a present result takes the present perfect; the past perfect needs a later past reference point.

questions.prompt: He ___ English for five years before he sat the CSS examination.
questions.explanation: An activity continuing up to an earlier past event takes the past perfect continuous; 'has been studying' cannot precede a past event.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: When 'taste' describes a quality it is stative and takes the simple present; the continuous form is wrong in this sense.

questions.prompt: Please do not disturb him; the chef ___ the soup at the moment.
questions.explanation: Here 'taste' is a deliberate action happening now, so the present continuous is used; 'tastes' would express a habit.

questions.prompt: How long ___ you known Ayesha? Since we were at school together.
questions.explanation: Duration up to now with a stative verb takes the present perfect ('have you known'); 'do you know' cannot express duration.

questions.prompt: The letter ___ yesterday by the postman.
questions.explanation: A finished past action in the passive takes 'was + past participle'; 'has been delivered' cannot be used with 'yesterday'.

questions.prompt: A new bridge ___ over the river at the moment.
questions.explanation: The bridge receives the action, so the present continuous passive is needed; 'is building' wrongly makes the bridge the builder.

questions.prompt: The results ___ before the students reached the hall.
questions.explanation: An earlier past action in the passive takes the past perfect passive; 'had announced' is active and lacks an object.

questions.prompt: I wish I ___ more time to prepare for the interview.
questions.explanation: 'Wish' about a present situation takes a past form ('had'); the present 'have' is not used after 'wish'.

questions.prompt: It is high time the authorities ___ action against smog.
questions.explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by a past tense with present meaning; the present 'take' is incorrect after this phrase.

questions.prompt: Hardly a day ___ without a power cut last summer.
questions.explanation: 'Last summer' fixes the time in the past, so the simple past is required; present forms contradict it.

questions.prompt: Since the new policy was introduced, exports ___ steadily.
questions.explanation: A trend continuing from a past point until now takes the present perfect continuous; 'are rising' cannot combine with 'since'.

questions.prompt: I ___ my homework, so I can go out now.
questions.explanation: A completed action relevant to the present takes the present perfect; the past perfect needs a past reference point.

questions.prompt: When the Prime Minister entered the hall, everyone ___ up.
questions.explanation: A completed reaction in a past narrative takes the simple past; present and future forms clash with 'entered'.

questions.prompt: This is the best biryani I ___.
questions.explanation: A superlative with 'ever' in a present frame takes the present perfect; 'had ever eaten' does not agree with 'This is'.

questions.prompt: My father ___ in the army for thirty years; he retired in 2010.
questions.explanation: The service ended in the past, so the simple past is correct; the present perfect would mean he is still serving.

questions.prompt: The Constitution of Pakistan ___ in 1973.
questions.explanation: A completed past event with a definite date takes the simple past passive; the present perfect cannot take a fixed past date.

questions.prompt: She ___ when the phone rang, so she did not answer it.
questions.explanation: An action in progress at a past moment takes the past continuous; 'slept' would not show that she was already asleep.

questions.prompt: By the time you read this letter, I ___ Pakistan.
questions.explanation: An action completed before a future moment takes the future perfect; 'have left' refers to the present.

questions.prompt: When he was a student, he ___ to the library every evening.
questions.explanation: A past habit that no longer exists is expressed by 'used to + base verb'; 'is used to' means 'accustomed to' and takes -ing.

questions.prompt: Hurry up and get on board; the train ___ leave.
questions.explanation: 'Be about to + base verb' expresses something on the point of happening; the other forms omit 'be' or 'to'.

questions.prompt: Scarcely ___ the hall when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: After 'scarcely' at the start, the past perfect is inverted ('had we entered'); normal word order is wrong here.

questions.prompt: She promised that she ___ the documents the next day.
questions.explanation: Future in the past after a past reporting verb uses 'would'; 'will send' breaks the sequence of tenses.

questions.prompt: ___ you be using the car this evening? I need it to visit my aunt.
questions.explanation: The future continuous 'Will you be using' politely asks about plans; 'Are you be' and the others are ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: I ___ for you for over an hour! Where have you been?
questions.explanation: Continuous waiting up to the present takes the present perfect continuous; 'had been waiting' needs a past reference point.

questions.prompt: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.explanation: A definite past time such as 'yesterday' requires the simple past; the present perfect cannot be used with it.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is correct?
options: He has been living here for five years.
He is living here since five years.
He has been living here since five years.
He lives here for five years.
questions.explanation: Duration up to now takes the present perfect (continuous) with 'for' + a period; 'since' needs a point in time.

questions.prompt: This time tomorrow, we ___ over the Arabian Sea.
questions.explanation: An action in progress at a definite future moment takes the future continuous; the other forms do not refer to that moment.

questions.prompt: Each time I ___ that song, I think of my village.
questions.explanation: Repeated present actions take the simple present in both clauses; 'heard' clashes with 'think' and 'will hear' is not used after 'each time'.

questions.prompt: It ___ since morning, and the streets are flooded.
questions.explanation: An action that began in the past and is still going on, with 'since', takes the present perfect continuous; 'is raining' cannot take 'since'.

questions.prompt: Did you ___ the minister's speech last night?
questions.explanation: After the auxiliary 'did', the main verb takes the base form; 'heard' doubles the past marking.

topics.title: Articles
topics.summary: When to use a, an, the or no article at all before a noun.

rules.rule: Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound. The sound matters, not the spelling.
examples: She waited for an hour at the bus stop.
He studies at a university in Faisalabad.

rules.rule: Use 'the' when the noun is specific, has already been mentioned, or is the only one of its kind.
examples: I bought a pen and a notebook. The pen has already run dry.
The moon was full last night.

rules.rule: Use no article with uncountable or plural nouns used in a general sense.
examples: Patience is a rare virtue.
Libraries play a vital role in education.

rules.rule: Use 'the' with rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts and plural country names, but not with most single countries, cities, lakes or individual mountains.
examples: The Ravi flows past Lahore.
K2 is in the Karakoram range.

rules.rule: Use 'the' with superlatives and ordinal numbers.
examples: It was the coldest night of the year.
She was the third speaker in the debate.

rules.rule: Many fixed expressions take no article: by train, by bus, at night, go to bed, go to school (as a pupil). Sports and meals in general also take no article.
examples: They travelled to Quetta by train.
We play hockey after lunch.

rules.rule: 'The' plus an adjective can refer to a whole group of people, and takes a plural verb.
examples: The elderly need better healthcare.
The rich should pay their fair share of tax.

questions.prompt: It took us ___ hour to reach the venue.
questions.explanation: 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so 'an' is required.

questions.prompt: Ali is ___ university lecturer in Peshawar.
questions.explanation: 'University' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so 'a' is used; a singular countable noun naming a profession needs an indefinite article.

questions.prompt: ___ Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
questions.explanation: Names of rivers take the definite article: the Indus.

questions.prompt: ___ honesty is the best policy.
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract, uncountable noun used in a general sense, so it takes no article.

questions.prompt: This is ___ tallest building in the city.
questions.explanation: Superlatives such as 'tallest' take the definite article.

questions.prompt: The government has announced new schemes to help ___ poor.
questions.explanation: 'The' plus an adjective (the poor) refers to a whole group of people.

questions.prompt: He travelled to Islamabad by ___ train.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression 'by + means of transport' (by train, by car, by air) takes no article.

questions.prompt: We went trekking in ___ Himalayas last summer.
questions.explanation: Mountain ranges take the definite article: the Himalayas.

questions.prompt: There was ___ one-sided debate in the Assembly yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'One' begins with a 'w' (consonant) sound, so 'a' is used; a newly introduced singular countable noun after 'There was' takes the indefinite article.

questions.prompt: Ahmed plays ___ cricket every Sunday.
questions.explanation: Names of sports and games take no article.

questions.prompt: Sana plays ___ violin beautifully.
questions.explanation: In British English, musical instruments played by someone take the definite article: play the violin, play the sitar.

questions.prompt: He was ___ first candidate to finish the paper.
questions.explanation: Ordinal numbers such as 'first' take the definite article.

questions.prompt: She is ___ honest officer.
questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a silent h and a vowel sound, so 'an' is used; 'a' goes before consonant sounds.

questions.prompt: He is ___ European diplomat, one of many posted in Islamabad.
questions.explanation: 'European' begins with a /j/ (consonant) sound, so 'a' is used, despite the vowel letter.

questions.prompt: Kamran wants to become ___ engineer.
questions.explanation: A singular countable profession takes an indefinite article, and 'engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an'.

questions.prompt: It was ___ unique opportunity to meet the President.
questions.explanation: 'Unique' begins with a /j/ sound, so it takes 'a'; 'an' is used only before vowel sounds.

questions.prompt: ___ Sun rises in the east.
questions.explanation: Things unique in our world, such as the Sun and the Moon, take 'the'.

questions.prompt: K2 is ___ second-highest mountain in the world.
questions.explanation: Ordinal and superlative expressions identify one item, so they take 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Arabian Sea lies to the south of Pakistan.
questions.explanation: Names of seas and oceans take 'the'; omitting it is incorrect.

questions.prompt: My father goes to ___ bed at ten o'clock every night.
questions.explanation: 'Go to bed' uses the zero article because it refers to the purpose (sleeping), not a particular bed.

questions.prompt: We usually have ___ breakfast at seven.
questions.explanation: Names of meals used in a general sense take no article; 'a breakfast' would need an adjective such as 'a big breakfast'.

questions.prompt: ___ Pakistan became independent in 1947.
questions.explanation: Most singular country names take no article; 'the' is used only for names such as 'the United Kingdom'.

questions.prompt: ___ United Kingdom has a parliamentary system of government.
questions.explanation: Country names containing words like 'Kingdom', 'States' or 'Republic' take 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Lake Saiful Muluk lies in the Kaghan Valley.
questions.explanation: Names of single lakes with the word 'Lake' first take no article.

questions.prompt: She bought ___ umbrella and ___ uniform.
questions.explanation: 'Umbrella' begins with a vowel sound (an), but 'uniform' begins with a /j/ sound (a).

questions.prompt: He has ___ MBA from a leading university.
questions.explanation: 'MBA' is read as 'em-bee-ay', starting with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

questions.prompt: The doctor ordered ___ X-ray of his chest.
questions.explanation: 'X' is pronounced 'eks', beginning with a vowel sound, so 'an' is used.

questions.prompt: I saw ___ old man near the gate. ___ man was carrying a heavy bag.
questions.explanation: A first mention takes the indefinite article ('an' before the vowel sound of 'old'); a second mention takes 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ elderly need special care during heatwaves.
questions.explanation: 'The' + adjective refers to a whole group of people and takes a plural verb.

questions.prompt: Ayesha is ___ only person who solved the puzzle.
questions.explanation: 'Only' identifies a single person, so it takes 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Prime Minister will address the nation tonight.
questions.explanation: There is only one Prime Minister of the country, so the title takes 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Gobi Desert stretches across Mongolia and China.
questions.explanation: Names of deserts take 'the'.

questions.prompt: He has ___ useful idea for the project.
questions.explanation: 'Useful' begins with a /j/ consonant sound, so it takes 'a'.

questions.prompt: Islamabad is ___ capital of Pakistan.
questions.explanation: A country has only one capital, so 'the' is required.

questions.prompt: ___ Shalimar Gardens in Lahore were laid out by Shah Jahan.
questions.explanation: Names of famous gardens with a plural noun take 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Mount Everest was first climbed in 1953.
questions.explanation: Names of single mountains take no article, unlike mountain ranges such as the Himalayas.

questions.prompt: She is studying in ___ Netherlands.
questions.explanation: Plural country names such as 'the Netherlands' take 'the'.

questions.prompt: The ship crossed ___ Atlantic in ten days.
questions.explanation: Names of oceans take 'the', even when the word 'Ocean' is omitted.

questions.prompt: The President flew to ___ Maldives for the summit.
questions.explanation: Groups of islands with plural names take 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ gold is a precious metal.
questions.explanation: Uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article.

questions.prompt: ___ milk on the table has gone sour.
questions.explanation: An uncountable noun made specific by a phrase ('on the table') takes 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ information you gave me was very useful.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'a' or 'an'; here it is specific, so 'the' is needed.

questions.prompt: He gave me ___ good advice before the interview.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'a' or 'many'; the zero article is correct.

questions.prompt: It is ___ unusual case.
questions.explanation: 'Unusual' begins with a vowel sound (/ʌ/), so it takes 'an'.

questions.prompt: She earns fifty thousand rupees ___ month.
questions.explanation: In rates and prices 'a' means 'per'; 'month' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a', not 'an'.

questions.prompt: The car was travelling at 120 kilometres ___ hour.
questions.explanation: In speeds 'a/an' means 'per'; 'hour' has a silent h, so it takes 'an'.

questions.prompt: What ___ beautiful view of the valley!
questions.explanation: In exclamations, 'what' + singular countable noun takes 'a/an'; 'beautiful' starts with a consonant sound.

questions.prompt: What ___ lovely weather we are having!
questions.explanation: 'Weather' is uncountable, so 'what' is followed directly by the adjective and noun with no article.

questions.prompt: Such ___ achievement deserves recognition.
questions.explanation: 'Such' + singular countable noun takes 'a/an'; 'achievement' begins with a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: He is quite ___ expert on constitutional law.
questions.explanation: 'Quite' is followed by 'a/an' with singular countable nouns, and 'expert' begins with a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: ___ Senate of Pakistan approved the bill unanimously.
questions.explanation: Names of unique national institutions take 'the'.

questions.prompt: I am reading ___ book you lent me.
questions.explanation: The relative clause 'you lent me' identifies a specific book, so 'the' is required.

questions.prompt: ___ Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
questions.explanation: Names of planets other than the Earth take no article.

questions.prompt: ___ English is widely used in Pakistan's courts and offices.
questions.explanation: Names of languages take no article; 'the' is used only in 'the English language'.

questions.prompt: ___ English are known for their love of tea.
questions.explanation: 'The' + nationality adjective (English, French, Dutch) refers to the people as a whole; without 'the' it means the language.

questions.prompt: I have ___ headache; may I leave early?
questions.explanation: Common ailments such as headache and cold take 'a'; 'headache' begins with a consonant sound.

questions.prompt: He is ___ heir to a large estate in Punjab.
questions.explanation: 'Heir' has a silent h and begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The Ravi flows through the Lahore.
questions.explanation: Rivers take 'the', but city names take no article.

questions.prompt: She signed ___ one-year contract with the ministry.
questions.explanation: 'One' begins with a /w/ consonant sound, so it takes 'a', not 'an'.

questions.prompt: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable, so it has no plural and cannot take 'a'; use 'some' or no article.

questions.prompt: ___ Moon looked unusually bright last night.
questions.explanation: The Moon is unique to us, so it takes 'the'.

questions.prompt: ___ Mughals ruled much of the subcontinent for over three centuries.
questions.explanation: Names of dynasties in the plural take 'the'.

questions.prompt: He has been ___ MP since 2018.
questions.explanation: 'MP' is read 'em-pee', beginning with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

questions.prompt: She has ___ eye for detail.
questions.explanation: 'Have an eye for' is a fixed phrase; 'eye' begins with a vowel sound, so 'an'.

topics.title: Prepositions
topics.summary: Choosing the correct preposition for time, place and movement, and the fixed prepositions that follow certain verbs, nouns and adjectives.

rules.rule: For time, use 'at' with clock times, 'on' with days and dates, and 'in' with months, years, seasons and parts of the day.
examples: The flight lands at 6.30 p.m.
Results are announced on 1 March, in the spring.

rules.rule: Use 'since' with a point in time and 'for' with a length of time, usually with perfect tenses.
examples: She has lived here since 2010.
She has lived here for fifteen years.

rules.rule: Many words take a fixed (dependent) preposition: accused of, comply with, prefer X to Y, based on, married to, interested in.
examples: He was accused of fraud.
I prefer walking to driving.

rules.rule: Use 'between' for two people or things and 'among' for more than two.
examples: The prize was shared between the two finalists.
There was disagreement among the committee members.

rules.rule: 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to.
examples: She sat beside her mother.
Besides Urdu, he speaks Pashto and Punjabi.

rules.rule: Some verbs take a direct object with no preposition: discuss, emphasise, enter, reach, resemble, request.
examples: We discussed the matter.
The train reached Rawalpindi at noon.

rules.rule: 'By' marks a deadline; 'until' (or 'till') marks a state that continues up to a point. 'Into' shows movement inwards; 'in' shows position.
examples: Submit the form by Monday. The office stays open until five.
He jumped into the river and stayed in the water for an hour.

questions.prompt: The exam will begin ___ 9 a.m.
questions.explanation: Clock times take the preposition 'at'.

questions.prompt: She was born ___ 14 August.
questions.explanation: Specific dates and days take the preposition 'on'.

questions.prompt: He has been working here ___ 2018.
questions.explanation: A starting point in time with a perfect tense takes 'since'; 'for' is used with a length of time.

questions.prompt: The official was accused ___ embezzlement.
questions.explanation: 'Accuse' takes the fixed preposition 'of': accused of a crime.

questions.prompt: The property was divided ___ the two brothers.
questions.explanation: 'Between' is used when two people or things are involved; 'among' is for more than two.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: The committee discussed about the proposal.
The committee discussed on the proposal.
The committee discussed over the proposal.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' takes a direct object with no preposition; 'a discussion about' is correct, but 'discuss about' is not.

questions.prompt: ___ English, she speaks French and Arabic.
questions.explanation: 'Besides' means 'in addition to'; 'beside' means 'next to'.

questions.prompt: Please submit the form ___ Friday; late applications will not be accepted.
questions.explanation: A deadline (no later than) is expressed with 'by'; 'until' and 'till' describe something continuing up to a point.

questions.prompt: I prefer tea ___ coffee.
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'prefer X to Y'; 'prefer than' is incorrect.

questions.prompt: He walked from the corridor ___ the room and closed the door behind him.
questions.explanation: Movement from outside to inside a place is shown by 'into'; 'in' shows position, not movement.

questions.prompt: The new rules must comply ___ the Constitution.
questions.explanation: 'Comply' takes the fixed preposition 'with'.

questions.prompt: The film is based ___ a true story.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'based on'.

questions.prompt: The shop is closed ___ Sundays.
questions.explanation: Days of the week take 'on'; 'in' is used for months, years and seasons.

questions.prompt: Pakistan won independence ___ 1947.
questions.explanation: Years take 'in'; 'on' is for days and dates.

questions.prompt: We will meet ___ the evening.
questions.explanation: Parts of the day (morning, afternoon, evening) take 'in'; the exception is 'at night'.

questions.prompt: She lives ___ Karachi.
questions.explanation: Cities and countries take 'in'; 'at' is used for a specific point or address.

questions.prompt: He lives ___ 12 Mall Road.
questions.explanation: A full address with a house number takes 'at'; 'on' can be used only with a street name alone.

questions.prompt: Several books were lying ___ the table.
questions.explanation: A surface takes 'on'; 'in' means inside an enclosed space.

questions.prompt: She has been ill ___ three days.
questions.explanation: 'For' is used with a period of time; 'since' needs a starting point such as 'Monday'.

questions.prompt: We arrived ___ Lahore late at night.
questions.explanation: 'Arrive in' is used with cities and countries; 'arrive to' is never correct.

questions.prompt: The plane arrived ___ the airport on time.
questions.explanation: 'Arrive at' is used with buildings and smaller places such as airports and stations.

questions.prompt: He is good ___ mathematics.
questions.explanation: Ability in a subject or skill is expressed with 'good at'; 'good in' is a common error.

questions.prompt: She is afraid ___ dogs.
questions.explanation: 'Afraid' takes 'of'; 'afraid from' is incorrect.

questions.prompt: He insisted ___ paying the bill.
questions.explanation: 'Insist' takes 'on' followed by a noun or gerund.

questions.prompt: I congratulate you ___ your success.
questions.explanation: In standard British English one congratulates someone 'on' an achievement; 'for' is a common error.

questions.prompt: The minister was absent ___ the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Absent' takes 'from'.

questions.prompt: He is married ___ a doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Married' takes 'to'; 'married with' is incorrect in this sense.

questions.prompt: She was angry ___ her brother for losing the keys.
questions.explanation: One is angry 'with' a person (and 'about' a thing).

questions.prompt: This book is quite different ___ that one.
questions.explanation: 'Different from' is the standard form; 'with', 'of' and 'by' are wrong after 'different'.

questions.prompt: The suspect was charged ___ theft.
questions.explanation: One is 'charged with' an offence, but 'accused of' it.

questions.prompt: She is fond ___ reading poetry.
questions.explanation: 'Fond' always takes 'of'.

questions.prompt: He is senior ___ me in the service.
questions.explanation: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', not 'than'.

questions.prompt: I am tired ___ hearing the same excuses.
questions.explanation: 'Tired of' means 'fed up with'; 'at' and 'by' cannot follow 'tired' in this sense.

questions.prompt: She has no objection ___ the proposal.
questions.explanation: 'Objection' takes 'to'.

questions.prompt: The success of the plan depends ___ public support.
questions.explanation: 'Depend' takes 'on' (or 'upon').

questions.prompt: The court acquitted her ___ all charges.
questions.explanation: 'Acquit' takes 'of'.

questions.prompt: The thieves broke ___ the house at midnight.
questions.explanation: 'Break into' expresses forced entry into a building; 'broke in the house' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: The new tunnel runs ___ the mountain.
questions.explanation: 'Through' means from one side to the other of something solid; 'between' and 'among' need two or more items.

questions.prompt: We walked ___ the bank of the Indus at sunset.
questions.explanation: 'Along' means following the length of something such as a road or riverbank.

questions.prompt: I have not seen him ___ last Eid.
questions.explanation: 'Since' marks the starting point of a period lasting until now; 'for' needs a length of time.

questions.prompt: The office is open ___ 9 a.m. ___ 5 p.m.
questions.explanation: The span of time is expressed by 'from ... to'; 'between' must pair with 'and'.

questions.prompt: We stayed at the hotel ___ the end of the month.
questions.explanation: 'Until' shows an action continuing up to a point; 'by' means 'not later than' and suits completed actions.

questions.prompt: ___ the meeting, his phone rang twice.
questions.explanation: 'During' is a preposition used before a noun; 'while' is a conjunction and needs a clause.

questions.prompt: He was born ___ a small village ___ Swat.
questions.explanation: Villages, districts and regions all take 'in'.

questions.prompt: He is waiting ___ the bus stop.
questions.explanation: A specific point such as a bus stop takes 'at'.

questions.prompt: We travelled the last mile ___ foot.
questions.explanation: 'On foot' is the fixed phrase, unlike 'by car' or 'by train'.

questions.prompt: He apologised ___ me ___ his rude behaviour.
questions.explanation: One apologises 'to' a person 'for' a fault.

questions.prompt: Every citizen is entitled ___ equal protection of the law.
questions.explanation: 'Entitled' takes 'to'.

questions.prompt: She takes great pride ___ her work.
questions.explanation: 'Take pride' is followed by 'in'.

questions.prompt: He prides himself ___ his punctuality.
questions.explanation: The verb 'pride oneself' takes 'on', unlike the noun phrase 'take pride in'.

questions.prompt: The new law will come ___ force next month.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'come into force'.

questions.prompt: ___ behalf of the staff, I thank you for your support.
questions.explanation: In British English the phrase is 'on behalf of'.

questions.prompt: ___ spite of the rain, the match continued.
questions.explanation: The phrase is 'in spite of'; it means the same as 'despite' (without 'of').

questions.prompt: The price of petrol has risen ___ ten rupees a litre.
questions.explanation: 'By' expresses the amount of an increase or decrease.

questions.prompt: The students listened ___ the lecture attentively.
questions.explanation: 'Listen' takes 'to' before its object.

questions.prompt: Please refrain ___ smoking in this building.
questions.explanation: 'Refrain' takes 'from'.

questions.prompt: She is suffering ___ a high fever.
questions.explanation: 'Suffer' from an illness takes 'from'.

questions.prompt: He was deprived ___ his rights.
questions.explanation: 'Deprive' takes 'of'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We discussed about the matter at length.
We discussed on the matter at length.
We discussed the matter at length.
We discussed over the matter at length.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' is transitive and takes a direct object with no preposition.

questions.prompt: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: He entered into the room quietly.
He entered in the room quietly.
He entered to the room quietly.
questions.explanation: 'Enter' meaning 'go into a place' takes a direct object; 'enter into' is used for agreements or discussions.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is correct?
options: She reached at Lahore on time.
She reached to Lahore on time.
She reached in Lahore on time.
questions.explanation: 'Reach' meaning 'arrive at' takes a direct object with no preposition.

questions.prompt: The flight was cancelled ___ account of the fog.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on account of', meaning 'because of'.

questions.prompt: The committee consists ___ seven members.
questions.explanation: 'Consist' meaning 'be made up of' takes 'of'.

questions.prompt: Translate this passage ___ Urdu.
questions.explanation: 'Translate' takes 'into' before the target language.

topics.title: Conjunctions
topics.summary: Using joining words correctly, including correlative pairs, subordinating conjunctions and fixed patterns such as no sooner ... than.

rules.rule: Coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join words or clauses of equal grammatical rank.
examples: The road was narrow but well maintained.
She applied early, so she got a seat.

rules.rule: Correlative pairs must be used as complete pairs: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, not only ... but also, whether ... or.
examples: Neither the driver nor the conductor was injured.
The scheme is not only costly but also impractical.

rules.rule: Do not pair 'although' with 'but', or 'because' with 'so'. One conjunction is enough to join two clauses.
examples: Although the hall was full, the speaker remained calm.
Because it was late, we took a taxi.

rules.rule: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it is not followed by another negative. 'Until' refers to time.
examples: You cannot enter unless you show your card.
Stay inside until the storm passes.

rules.rule: Fixed patterns: no sooner ... than; hardly / scarcely ... when; so + adjective ... that; such + noun phrase ... that.
examples: No sooner had the train stopped than the passengers poured out.
It was such a long speech that people began to leave.

rules.rule: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and is followed by 'should' or the base form of the verb.
examples: Speak softly lest you wake the baby.
He kept a copy lest the original should be lost.

rules.rule: Linking adverbs such as however, therefore and moreover connect ideas between clauses but are not conjunctions; use a semicolon or full stop before them.
examples: The plan was bold; however, it lacked funding.
Prices rose sharply. Therefore, demand fell.

questions.prompt: ___ he was exhausted, he continued working late into the night.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a contrast between being exhausted and continuing to work; 'But' cannot begin a subordinate clause like this.

questions.prompt: Neither the manager ___ his deputy attended the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' must be paired with 'nor'.

questions.prompt: No sooner had the bell rung ___ the students rushed out.
questions.explanation: The fixed pattern is 'no sooner ... than'.

questions.prompt: Hardly had she sat down ___ the phone rang.
questions.explanation: The fixed pattern is 'hardly ... when'; 'than' belongs with 'no sooner'.

questions.prompt: You will fail the test ___ you work harder.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': you will fail if you do not work harder.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Although he is rich, he is unhappy.
Although he is rich, but he is unhappy.
Although rich, but he is unhappy.
He is rich, although but he is unhappy.
questions.explanation: 'Although' and 'but' must not be used together; one conjunction is enough to join the two clauses.

questions.prompt: She is not only intelligent ___ hard-working.
questions.explanation: The correlative pair is 'not only ... but also'.

questions.prompt: Walk carefully on the icy path ___ you should slip.
questions.explanation: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and is followed by 'should' plus the base verb.

questions.prompt: The lecture was ___ dull that half the audience fell asleep.
questions.explanation: An adjective on its own (dull) takes 'so ... that'; 'such ... that' needs a noun phrase.

questions.prompt: Wait here ___ I come back.
questions.explanation: 'Until' marks the point in time up to which the waiting continues.

questions.prompt: You can ___ pay online or deposit the fee at the bank.
questions.explanation: 'Or' pairs with 'either' to offer a choice between two alternatives.

questions.prompt: He is honest; ___, he is not very efficient.
questions.explanation: The second clause contrasts with the first, so the linking adverb 'however' is needed.

questions.prompt: I wanted to attend the lecture, ___ I was too ill.
questions.explanation: 'But' joins contrasting clauses; 'so' would wrongly present the illness as a result.

questions.prompt: Hurry up, ___ you will miss the train.
questions.explanation: 'Or' after an imperative means 'otherwise', introducing a warning; 'and' would wrongly suggest hurrying causes missing the train.

questions.prompt: She studied hard, ___ she passed with distinction.
questions.explanation: 'So' introduces a result; 'but' and 'yet' signal a contrast that is not present.

questions.prompt: He is wealthy, ___ he is not content.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' joins contrasting ideas; 'so' would wrongly make discontent a result of wealth.

questions.prompt: He did not attend the meeting, ___ did he send an apology.
questions.explanation: 'Nor' adds a further negative and is followed by inversion ('did he'); 'or' cannot be followed by inversion.

questions.prompt: Both the Senate ___ the National Assembly approved the amendment.
questions.explanation: The correlative pair is 'both ... and'; 'or' and 'nor' belong to 'either' and 'neither'.

questions.prompt: Either you apologise ___ you leave the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Either' pairs with 'or'; 'nor' pairs only with 'neither'.

questions.prompt: He asked me ___ I had finished the report.
questions.explanation: Reported yes/no questions are introduced by 'whether' (or 'if'); 'that' introduces statements.

questions.prompt: The match went ahead ___ it was raining heavily.
questions.explanation: 'Even though' introduces a strong contrast; 'because' would wrongly make the rain the reason.

questions.prompt: He was late ___ his car broke down.
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces a reason; 'although' signals a contrast that is not present.

questions.prompt: She saved money ___ she could buy a laptop.
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces purpose; 'in order' needs 'to' or 'that'.

questions.prompt: ___ you leave now, you will miss the flight.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': if you do not leave now, you will miss it; 'because' gives an illogical reason.

questions.prompt: I will not sign the document ___ I have read it carefully.
questions.explanation: 'Not ... until' means the action will happen only after a certain point.

questions.prompt: Take notes during the lecture ___ you forget the main points.
questions.explanation: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and introduces something to be avoided; 'unless' means 'if not'.

questions.prompt: He speaks ___ he were an expert on the subject.
questions.explanation: 'As if' introduces an unreal comparison and is often followed by 'were'.

questions.prompt: ___ I was walking home, I met an old friend.
questions.explanation: 'While' introduces an action in progress during another event.

questions.prompt: He is ___ intelligent ___ hard-working.
questions.explanation: Correlative pairs must match: 'both ... and'; 'not only' pairs with 'but also'.

questions.prompt: Not only did he win the debate, ___ he also set a new record.
questions.explanation: 'Not only' pairs with 'but (also)'; 'and' breaks the correlative pair.

questions.prompt: She would rather resign ___ compromise her principles.
questions.explanation: 'Would rather' is followed by 'than' in comparisons; 'then' is an adverb of time.

questions.prompt: It was such a hot day ___ the schools were closed.
questions.explanation: 'Such ... that' introduces a result clause.

questions.prompt: Bilal is as tall ___ his father.
questions.explanation: Equal comparison uses 'as ... as'; 'than' follows comparative adjectives such as 'taller'.

questions.prompt: I have known him ___ he was a child.
questions.explanation: 'Since' introduces the starting point of a situation continuing to now; 'for' is a preposition used with periods.

questions.prompt: You may go out ___ you finish your homework first.
questions.explanation: 'Provided that' introduces a condition that must be met; 'unless' would reverse the meaning.

questions.prompt: Aslam works hard, ___ his brother is rather lazy.
questions.explanation: 'Whereas' contrasts two facts; 'because' wrongly suggests one causes the other.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Although he was ill, he went to work.
Although he was ill but he went to work.
Despite he was ill, he went to work.
Although ill, but he went to work.
questions.explanation: 'Although' already shows contrast, so 'but' must not be added; 'despite' is a preposition and cannot take a clause.

questions.prompt: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.
options: The reason he resigned is because of he was unwell.
The reason he resigned is that he was unwell.
The reason he resigned is due he was unwell.
The reason he resigned is as he was unwell.
questions.explanation: After 'the reason ... is', a 'that' clause is required; 'because of' cannot be followed by a clause.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is correct?
options: Unless you work hard, you will fail.
Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
Unless you will work hard, you will fail.
Unless you don't work hard, you will not fail.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it takes a positive verb in the present tense; adding 'not' creates a double negative.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that is correct.
options: Scarcely had he arrived than the meeting began.
Scarcely he had arrived when the meeting began.
Scarcely had he arrived when the meeting began.
Scarcely had he arrived then the meeting began.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely' takes 'when' (not 'than') and requires inversion ('had he').

questions.prompt: Poor ___ he is, he never begs for help.
questions.explanation: In the concessive pattern 'adjective + as + clause', 'as' means 'although'.

questions.prompt: I will lend you the book ___ you return it by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'As long as' introduces a condition; 'unless' would reverse the meaning.

questions.prompt: ___ it rains or shines, the parade will go ahead.
questions.explanation: 'Whether ... or' introduces two alternatives that make no difference; 'either' cannot introduce a clause like this.

questions.prompt: We stayed indoors, ___ it was raining heavily.
questions.explanation: The coordinating conjunction 'for' means 'because' in formal English; 'yet' signals contrast.

questions.prompt: Not only ___ the exam, but she also won a scholarship.
questions.explanation: When 'not only' begins a clause, the subject and auxiliary are inverted ('did she pass').

questions.prompt: ___ had I opened the door than the cat rushed in.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than'; 'hardly' and 'scarcely' pair with 'when'.

questions.prompt: ___ you have submitted the form, you cannot change it.
questions.explanation: 'Once' means 'as soon as' or 'after'; 'unless' would make the sentence illogical.

questions.prompt: I am happy to help you ___ I can.
questions.explanation: 'Whenever' means 'at any time that'; 'unless' and 'lest' make the sentence illogical.

questions.prompt: Take an umbrella ___ it rains.
questions.explanation: 'In case' means 'as a precaution against the possibility that'; 'unless' would mean 'if it does not rain'.

questions.prompt: ___ he was a child, he lived in Quetta.
questions.explanation: 'When' introduces a time clause; the others do not express time.

questions.prompt: The report was thorough, ___ it was far too long.
questions.explanation: 'But' introduces a contrast between a good and a bad quality; 'so' would present length as a result.

questions.prompt: Do the work properly ___ do not do it at all.
questions.explanation: 'Or' offers an alternative; 'nor' must follow a negative clause.

questions.prompt: It was ___ a difficult paper that many candidates left early.
questions.explanation: 'Such' is used before 'a/an + adjective + noun'; 'so' goes directly before an adjective.

questions.prompt: ___ hard he tries, he cannot pass the driving test.
questions.explanation: 'However' + adjective/adverb means 'no matter how'; 'although' cannot be followed directly by 'hard'.

questions.prompt: He agreed to the plan, ___ reluctantly.
questions.explanation: 'Albeit' means 'although' and can introduce an adverb or phrase; 'despite' needs a noun.

questions.prompt: Inasmuch ___ he is the eldest, the decision is his.
questions.explanation: The fixed conjunction is 'inasmuch as', meaning 'since' or 'because'.

questions.prompt: Now ___ the exams are over, we can relax.
questions.explanation: 'Now that' means 'because now'; 'then' is an adverb, not part of this conjunction.

questions.prompt: She will attend the wedding only ___ she is invited.
questions.explanation: 'Only if' states the sole condition; 'until' would wrongly express time.

questions.prompt: We must act now; ___, it will be too late.
questions.explanation: 'Otherwise' means 'if not' and links two clauses separated by a semicolon; 'unless' needs a clause after it.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: You can either take the bus nor walk.
You can either take the bus or walk.
You can either take the bus and walk.
You can neither take the bus or walk.
questions.explanation: 'Either' pairs with 'or', and 'neither' with 'nor'; mixed pairs are wrong.

questions.prompt: Pick the correct sentence.
options: Both Ali as well as Sara were present.
Both Ali or Sara were present.
Both Ali and Sara were present.
Both Ali nor Sara were present.
questions.explanation: 'Both' must pair with 'and'; 'both ... as well as' is a common error.

questions.prompt: ___ you have finished your work, you may go home.
questions.explanation: Here 'since' means 'because'; 'unless' and 'until' make the sentence illogical.

questions.prompt: I do not know ___ to laugh or cry.
questions.explanation: Only 'whether' can be followed by a to-infinitive; 'if to laugh' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: The army will remain on alert ___ the floodwaters recede.
questions.explanation: 'Until' marks the point at which the situation will end.

topics.title: Phrasal Verbs
topics.summary: Common verb-plus-particle combinations, what they mean and where the object goes.

rules.rule: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle (such as up, off, out) whose meaning often differs from the verb alone.
examples: She gave up smoking. (stopped)
The plane took off at dawn. (left the ground)

rules.rule: With separable phrasal verbs, a noun object can go before or after the particle, but a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle.
examples: Switch off the fan. / Switch the fan off.
Switch it off. (not: Switch off it.)

rules.rule: With inseparable phrasal verbs, the object always comes after the whole verb.
examples: Who will look after the children?
The police are looking into the theft.

rules.rule: Some phrasal verbs take no object at all.
examples: The bus broke down near Sukkur.
We set off before sunrise.

rules.rule: Three-part phrasal verbs are never separated: put up with, look forward to, come up with, run out of.
examples: We have run out of paper.
I look forward to hearing from you.

rules.rule: In 'look forward to' and 'object to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not the base verb.
examples: She is looking forward to joining the service.
They objected to paying the fine.

questions.prompt: The meeting has been ___ until next week because the chairman is ill.
questions.explanation: 'Put off' means to postpone.

questions.prompt: The firefighters took two hours to ___ the blaze.
questions.explanation: 'Put out' means to extinguish a fire.

questions.prompt: I cannot ___ his rude behaviour any longer.
questions.explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate.

questions.prompt: Her car ___ on the motorway, so she was late.
questions.explanation: 'Break down' means to stop working, as a machine or vehicle does.

questions.prompt: Cholera ___ in several flood-affected villages.
questions.explanation: 'Break out' means to start suddenly, used of diseases, fires and wars.

questions.prompt: We are looking forward to ___ you at the ceremony.
questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by an -ing form.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: 'Turn off' is separable, and a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle.

questions.prompt: The committee will ___ the complaint and report back within a week.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means to investigate.

questions.prompt: Children who ___ their teachers usually try to copy their good habits.
questions.explanation: 'Look up to' means to admire or respect, which explains why the children copy their teachers.

questions.prompt: The strike was ___ after the government agreed to the union's demands.
questions.explanation: 'Call off' means to cancel.

questions.prompt: After months of experiments, the researchers ___ an ingenious method of purifying water.
questions.explanation: 'Come up with' means to think of or produce an idea or plan.

questions.prompt: He ___ his father in both looks and temperament.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' means to resemble an older family member.

questions.prompt: The government has decided to ___ funds for flood relief in next year's budget.
questions.explanation: 'Set aside' means to reserve something for a particular purpose; 'set off' means to start a journey or cause to explode.

questions.prompt: Industrialisation ___ profound changes in the social structure of the subcontinent.
questions.explanation: 'Bring about' means to cause something to happen; 'bring up' means to raise a child or mention a topic.

questions.prompt: The survey team will ___ a detailed study of groundwater levels in Thar.
questions.explanation: 'Carry out' means to perform or conduct a task; 'carry off' means to win or to take away by force.

questions.prompt: Talks between the two parties ___ when neither side would compromise.
questions.explanation: 'Break down' means to fail or collapse, as negotiations do; 'break out' means to start suddenly, as a war or fire does.

questions.prompt: After weeks of protest, the management finally ___ and accepted the workers' demands.
questions.explanation: 'Give in' means to yield or surrender; 'give off' means to emit a smell, heat or light.

questions.prompt: The ministry ___ his application because it was incomplete.
questions.explanation: 'Turn down' means to reject; 'turn up' means to arrive or appear.

questions.prompt: He worked late every evening to ___ the time he had lost during his illness.
questions.explanation: 'Make up for' means to compensate for something lost; 'make off with' means to steal and run away.

questions.prompt: Some people ___ those who do manual labour, an attitude that is both unjust and unwise.
questions.explanation: 'Look down upon' means to regard as inferior, which the words 'unjust and unwise' confirm; 'look up to' means to admire.

questions.prompt: Villagers had to ___ frequent power cuts throughout the summer.
questions.explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate; 'put off' means to postpone.

questions.prompt: The Second World War ___ in September 1939.
questions.explanation: 'Break out' is used for the sudden start of a war, fire or epidemic; 'break down' means to stop working or collapse.

questions.prompt: The flight to Islamabad ___ on time despite the fog.
questions.explanation: 'Take off' means (of an aircraft) to leave the ground; 'take over' means to assume control.

questions.prompt: After retiring, she ___ Urdu calligraphy as a hobby.
questions.explanation: 'Take up' means to begin a new activity or hobby; 'take down' means to write down or dismantle.

questions.prompt: The doctor advised him to ___ smoking immediately.
questions.explanation: 'Give up' means to stop a habit; 'give in' means to surrender to pressure and takes no object here.

questions.prompt: Rotting garbage ___ an unpleasant smell.
questions.explanation: 'Give off' means to emit a smell, gas or heat; 'give up' means to abandon a habit or attempt.

questions.prompt: Our supplies of clean water ___ on the third day of the flood.
questions.explanation: 'Run out' means to be used up completely; 'run into' means to meet by chance or collide with.

questions.prompt: While shopping in Anarkali, I ___ an old school friend.
questions.explanation: 'Run into' means to meet someone unexpectedly; 'run over' means to knock down with a vehicle.

questions.prompt: The police are ___ the cause of the explosion.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means to investigate; 'look after' means to take care of.

questions.prompt: Young cricketers ___ senior players who show discipline and sportsmanship.
questions.explanation: 'Look up to' means to admire and respect; 'look down on' means to regard as inferior.

questions.prompt: The speaker talked so fast that I could not ___ what he was saying.
questions.explanation: 'Make out' means to understand or perceive with difficulty; 'make up' means to invent or to reconcile.

questions.prompt: The thief ___ the jewellery before the guards arrived.
questions.explanation: 'Make off with' means to steal and escape; 'make up for' means to compensate.

questions.prompt: The committee ___ new rules to curb tax evasion.
questions.explanation: 'Draw up' means to prepare a formal document or plan; 'draw on' means to make use of a resource.

questions.prompt: These customs have been ___ from generation to generation.
questions.explanation: 'Hand down' means to pass on to the next generation; 'hand in' means to submit.

questions.prompt: The chief engineer ___ after twenty years of service.
questions.explanation: 'Step down' means to resign or retire from a post; 'step up' means to increase.

questions.prompt: The cricket match was ___ because of the heavy rain.
questions.explanation: 'Call off' means to cancel; 'call on' means to visit.

questions.prompt: The Prime Minister ___ the President at Aiwan-e-Sadr yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Call on' means to pay a formal visit; 'call off' means to cancel.

questions.prompt: The situation ___ immediate action from the government.
questions.explanation: 'Call for' means to require or demand; 'call on' means to visit or formally ask a person.

questions.prompt: Burglars ___ the house while the family was away.
questions.explanation: 'Break into' means to enter a building illegally by force; 'break out' means to start suddenly or escape.

questions.prompt: Schools in Punjab ___ for the winter holidays in late December.
questions.explanation: In British English, 'break up' means (of a school) to close for the holidays; 'break out' means to start suddenly.

questions.prompt: The cost of living has ___ steeply this year.
questions.explanation: 'Go up' means to rise or increase; 'go off' means to explode, ring or turn bad.

questions.prompt: Throw that milk away; it has ___.
questions.explanation: In British English, 'go off' means (of food) to become bad; 'go up' means to rise.

questions.prompt: After missing a month of classes, she worked hard to ___ with her classmates.
questions.explanation: 'Catch up with' means to reach the same level as others; 'catch on' means to become popular or to understand.

questions.prompt: The engineers ___ the old bridge and built a new one.

questions.prompt: It ___ that the documents had been forged.
questions.explanation: 'Turn out' means to prove to be the case; 'turn down' means to reject.

questions.prompt: During the recession the factory had to ___ two hundred workers.
questions.explanation: 'Lay off' means to dismiss workers because there is not enough work; 'lay down' means to establish a rule.

questions.prompt: The Constitution ___ the fundamental rights of every citizen.
questions.explanation: 'Lay down' means to establish a rule or principle formally; 'lay off' means to dismiss workers.

questions.prompt: The government plans to ___ a new university in Gilgit.
questions.explanation: 'Set up' means to establish; 'set off' means to begin a journey.

questions.prompt: Delays in funding ___ the project by two years.
questions.explanation: 'Set back' means to delay progress; 'set off' means to start a journey or trigger something.

questions.explanation: 'Pass away' is a polite way of saying 'die'; 'pass out' means to faint or, in British English, to graduate from a military academy.
