topics.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
topics.summary: Making the verb agree in number with its true subject, including tricky cases such as either/or, each and a number of.

rules.rule: The verb agrees with the head of the subject, not with a noun inside a phrase that comes between them.
examples: The cost of the new buses is very high.
A bundle of old letters was found in the attic.

rules.rule: Phrases such as as well as, along with and together with do not change the number of the subject; the verb agrees with the first noun.
examples: The captain, along with his players, was cheered.
The students, as well as their teacher, were late.

rules.rule: With either ... or and neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it.
examples: Either the clerks or the officer is responsible.
Neither the officer nor the clerks are responsible.

rules.rule: Each, every, everyone, everybody, no one and either or neither used alone take a singular verb.
examples: Each of the houses has a garden.
Everyone was invited.

rules.rule: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb; 'the number of' refers to a single figure and takes a singular verb.
examples: A number of complaints have been received.
The number of complaints has doubled.

rules.rule: Nouns ending in -s such as news, economics and mathematics are singular, and an amount of money, time or distance seen as one unit takes a singular verb.
examples: Mathematics was his weakest subject.
Five kilometres is a long way to walk in this heat.

questions.prompt: The list of successful candidates ___ been posted on the notice board.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'list' (singular), not 'candidates', so the singular 'has' is required.

questions.prompt: The principal, as well as the teachers, ___ present at the ceremony.
questions.explanation: 'As well as' does not make the subject plural; the verb agrees with 'the principal'.

questions.prompt: Neither the students nor the teacher ___ aware of the change.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the teacher' (singular).

questions.prompt: Each of the candidates ___ given a roll number.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes a singular verb, even when followed by 'of' plus a plural noun.

questions.prompt: A number of applicants ___ been shortlisted.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb.

questions.prompt: The number of road accidents ___ risen sharply this year.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' refers to a single figure and takes a singular verb.

questions.prompt: Economics ___ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -s, such as economics, are singular.

questions.prompt: Ten thousand rupees ___ too much for a single textbook.
questions.explanation: An amount of money regarded as one sum takes a singular verb.

questions.prompt: Either my brothers or my sister ___ going to collect the parcel.
questions.explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'my sister' (singular).

questions.prompt: Everyone in the hostel ___ to switch off the lights by eleven.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.prompt: The news from the flood-hit areas ___ distressing.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and is always singular.

questions.prompt: The quality of the roads in these districts ___ poor.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'quality' (singular); 'roads' and 'districts' are inside the prepositional phrase.

questions.prompt: Bread and butter ___ his usual breakfast.
questions.explanation: Two nouns joined by 'and' that express a single idea take a singular verb; 'are' wrongly treats 'bread and butter' as two separate things.

questions.prompt: Slow and steady ___ the race.
questions.explanation: 'Slow and steady' expresses one idea, so it takes a singular verb; 'win' is the plural form.

questions.prompt: Physics ___ taught by Mr Farooq in the second term.
questions.explanation: Subjects ending in -ics, such as physics, are singular; 'are' wrongly treats the word as plural.

questions.prompt: The committee ___ submitted its report to the Senate.
questions.explanation: A collective noun acting as a single unit (shown by 'its') takes a singular verb; 'have' would clash with 'its'.

questions.prompt: The cattle ___ grazing on the banks of the canal.
questions.explanation: 'Cattle' is always plural, so it takes a plural verb; 'is' treats it as singular.

questions.prompt: The police ___ arrested the main suspect.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun and takes a plural verb; 'has' treats it as singular.

questions.prompt: Not only the minister but also his advisers ___ responsible for the delay.
questions.explanation: With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'advisers', which is plural; 'is' agrees wrongly with 'minister'.

questions.prompt: The teacher, with all her students, ___ visiting the Lahore Museum today.
questions.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'with' does not change the number of the subject, so 'the teacher' takes 'is'; 'are' wrongly counts the students.

questions.prompt: Each boy and each girl ___ a certificate at the end of the course.
questions.explanation: When nouns joined by 'and' are each preceded by 'each' or 'every', the verb is singular; 'receive' is plural.

questions.prompt: Many a student ___ failed this paper because of poor time management.
questions.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb; 'have' is plural.

questions.prompt: The Arabian Nights ___ a famous collection of stories.
questions.explanation: The title of a single book takes a singular verb even when it is plural in form; 'are' treats the title as plural.

questions.prompt: Two-thirds of the land in the district ___ under cultivation.
questions.explanation: With fractions, the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'; 'land' is uncountable, so 'is' is correct and 'are' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Two-thirds of the voters ___ in favour of the bill.
questions.explanation: With fractions, the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'; 'voters' is plural, so 'is' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Half of the cake ___ already been eaten.
questions.explanation: 'Half of' takes the number of the following noun; 'cake' is singular here, so 'have' is wrong.

questions.prompt: None of the information in the report ___ reliable.
questions.explanation: 'None of' followed by an uncountable noun such as 'information' takes a singular verb; 'are' is wrong.

questions.prompt: The furniture in these offices ___ very old.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb; the plural 'offices' in the phrase does not affect it.

questions.prompt: The scissors ___ on the table in the staff room.
questions.explanation: Nouns for things with two parts, such as scissors, are plural; 'is' treats them as singular.

questions.prompt: A pair of scissors ___ on the table in the staff room.
questions.explanation: With 'a pair of', the subject is 'pair', which is singular; 'are' wrongly agrees with 'scissors'.

questions.prompt: The rich ___ not always happy.
questions.explanation: 'The' + adjective referring to a class of people is plural; 'is' treats it as singular.

questions.prompt: One of my cousins ___ a doctor in Peshawar.
questions.explanation: In 'one of + plural noun', the subject is 'one', so the verb is singular; 'are' wrongly agrees with 'cousins'.

questions.prompt: The majority of the members ___ against the motion yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'The majority of' followed by a plural noun takes a plural verb, and 'yesterday' requires the past tense, so only 'were' fits.

questions.prompt: Every one of the windows ___ broken during the storm.
questions.explanation: 'Every one of' takes a singular verb because the subject is 'one'; 'were' wrongly agrees with 'windows'.

questions.prompt: The poet and philosopher ___ been honoured by the nation.
questions.explanation: When one article precedes two nouns joined by 'and', they refer to one person, so the verb is singular; 'have' implies two people.

questions.prompt: The secretary and the treasurer ___ been elected unopposed.
questions.explanation: When each noun has its own article, two different people are meant and the verb is plural; 'has' implies one person.

questions.prompt: Either you or he ___ to blame for this mistake.
questions.explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'he', which takes 'is'; 'are' agrees wrongly with 'you'.

questions.prompt: Neither he nor I ___ ready to sign the agreement.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'I', which takes 'am'; 'is' agrees wrongly with 'he'.

questions.prompt: The ship, with its entire crew, ___ lost at sea.
questions.explanation: A phrase beginning with 'with' does not change the number of the subject 'the ship'; 'were' wrongly counts the crew.

questions.prompt: Gold, like silver, ___ a precious metal.
questions.explanation: Words added by 'like' do not form a compound subject, so 'gold' takes a singular verb; 'are' wrongly counts silver.

questions.prompt: What he says and what he does ___ never the same.
questions.explanation: Two noun clauses joined by 'and' referring to different things form a plural subject; 'is' treats them as one.

questions.prompt: Measles ___ spread rapidly through the relief camps.
questions.explanation: Disease names such as measles are singular despite the final -s; 'have' is plural.

questions.prompt: Five years ___ a long time to wait for justice.
questions.explanation: A period of time considered as one amount takes a singular verb; 'are' treats the years separately.

questions.prompt: Somebody ___ left the main gate open.
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronouns such as 'somebody' are singular; 'have' is plural.

questions.prompt: Everybody in the department ___ the new director.
questions.explanation: 'Everybody' is singular and takes a singular verb; 'respect' is the plural form.

questions.prompt: The children, along with their mother, ___ gone to Quetta for the holidays.
questions.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'along with' does not affect the subject 'children', which is plural; 'has' agrees wrongly with 'mother'.

questions.prompt: Rice, as well as wheat, ___ grown in Punjab.
questions.explanation: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject, 'rice', which is singular; 'are' wrongly adds wheat to the subject.

questions.prompt: A lot of time ___ been wasted on pointless meetings.
questions.explanation: 'A lot of' takes the number of the following noun; 'time' is uncountable, so 'have' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Mr Khan's family ___ arguing among themselves about the inheritance.
questions.explanation: A collective noun whose members act individually (shown by 'themselves') takes a plural verb; 'is' would clash with 'themselves'.

questions.prompt: These phenomena ___ difficult to explain.
questions.explanation: 'Phenomena' is the plural of 'phenomenon' and takes a plural verb; 'is' treats it as singular.

questions.prompt: The criteria for selection ___ been revised this year.
questions.explanation: 'Criteria' is the plural of 'criterion' and takes a plural verb; 'has' treats it as singular.

questions.prompt: His only source of income ___ the rent from two shops.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject 'source', not with the complement after it; 'are' wrongly agrees with 'two shops'.

questions.prompt: The main cause of last year's floods ___ unusually heavy monsoon rain.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject 'cause', which is singular, and 'last year's' requires the past tense; 'were' is plural.

questions.prompt: Twenty per cent of the budget ___ allocated to education.
questions.explanation: With percentages, the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'; 'budget' is singular, so 'are' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Twenty per cent of the students ___ absent today.
questions.explanation: With percentages, the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'; 'students' is plural, so 'is' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Neither the minister nor his secretaries ___ available for comment yesterday.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'secretaries', which is plural, and 'yesterday' needs the past tense; 'was' is singular.

questions.prompt: Each of the provinces ___ its own assembly.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' is followed by a singular verb because the subject is 'each'; 'have' wrongly agrees with 'provinces'.

questions.prompt: Either of these roads ___ to Abbottabad.
questions.explanation: 'Either' as a subject is singular, so it takes 'leads'; 'lead' is the plural form.

questions.prompt: Every man, woman and child ___ entitled to free treatment in this hospital.
questions.explanation: When subjects joined by 'and' are preceded by 'every', the verb is singular; 'are' is plural.

questions.prompt: Statistics ___ a compulsory paper for students of economics at this university.
questions.explanation: 'Statistics' as the name of a subject is singular; 'are' would be right only when it means a set of figures.

questions.prompt: These statistics on child labour ___ alarming.
questions.explanation: 'Statistics' meaning a set of figures is plural; 'is' would be right only for the name of the subject.

questions.prompt: The houses that were damaged in the earthquake ___ been rebuilt.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the houses', which is plural; 'has' wrongly agrees with 'earthquake'.

questions.prompt: Few students ___ the answer to this question.
questions.explanation: 'Few' is plural and takes a plural verb; 'knows' is singular.

questions.prompt: Little ___ known about the poet's early life.
questions.explanation: 'Little' refers to an uncountable quantity and takes a singular verb; 'are' is plural.

topics.title: Active and Passive Voice
topics.summary: Changing sentences between the active and passive voice while keeping the tense and meaning unchanged.

rules.rule: The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive. The passive is formed with a form of 'be' plus the past participle.
examples: Active: The council built the bridge.
Passive: The bridge was built by the council.

rules.rule: Keep the original tense by changing only the form of 'be': is made, is being made, has been made, was made, had been made, will be made.
examples: They are repairing the road. → The road is being repaired.
They have repaired the road. → The road has been repaired.

rules.rule: With modal verbs, use modal + be + past participle.
examples: You should check the figures. → The figures should be checked.
We can solve the problem. → The problem can be solved.

rules.rule: Only transitive verbs (verbs with an object) can be made passive. Verbs such as arrive, sleep and happen have no passive form.
examples: The guests arrived late. (no passive form)
The judge dismissed the case. → The case was dismissed by the judge.

rules.rule: The agent ('by ...') can be left out when it is unknown, obvious or unimportant.
examples: Someone has broken the window. → The window has been broken.
The thief was arrested (by the police).

rules.rule: Imperatives become passive with 'Let ... be + past participle'; questions keep question order with the auxiliary before the subject.
examples: Shut the gate. → Let the gate be shut.
Did they sign the treaty? → Was the treaty signed by them?

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The clerk types the letters.
options: The letters are typed by the clerk.
The letters were typed by the clerk.
The letters are being typed by the clerk.
The letters have typed by the clerk.
questions.explanation: The simple present active becomes 'am/is/are + past participle' in the passive; the tense must not change.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The police are investigating the case.
options: The case is investigated by the police.
The case is being investigated by the police.
The case has been investigated by the police.
The case was being investigated by the police.
questions.explanation: The present continuous becomes 'is/are being + past participle' in the passive.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The board has approved the budget.
options: The budget was approved by the board.
The budget is approved by the board.
The budget has been approved by the board.
The budget had approved by the board.
questions.explanation: The present perfect becomes 'has/have been + past participle' in the passive.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: Someone stole my wallet.
questions.explanation: The simple past becomes 'was/were + past participle'; the unknown agent 'someone' is dropped.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: They will announce the results tomorrow.
options: The results will be announced tomorrow.
The results would be announced tomorrow.
The results will have been announced tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The simple future becomes 'will be + past participle' in the passive.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: You must submit the application before Friday.
options: The application must submit before Friday.
The application must be submitted before Friday.
The application must have been submitted before Friday.
The application must be submit before Friday.
questions.explanation: With a modal verb, the passive is 'modal + be + past participle'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: Who wrote this report?
options: By whom this report was written?
By whom was this report written?
By whom has this report been written?
questions.explanation: 'Who' as subject becomes 'By whom', and the question keeps the auxiliary before the subject; the simple past must not change.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: Close the door.
questions.explanation: An imperative becomes passive with 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The engineers had completed the bridge before the monsoon.
options: The bridge had been completed by the engineers before the monsoon.
The bridge was completed by the engineers before the monsoon.
The bridge has been completed by the engineers before the monsoon.
The bridge had completed by the engineers before the monsoon.
questions.explanation: The past perfect becomes 'had been + past participle' in the passive.

questions.prompt: Which sentence CANNOT be changed into the passive voice?
questions.explanation: 'Arrive' is intransitive (it has no object), so it has no passive form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: Did the minister inaugurate the hospital?
options: Did the hospital inaugurated by the minister?
Has the hospital been inaugurated by the minister?
Was the hospital inaugurated by the minister?
Was the hospital being inaugurated by the minister?
questions.explanation: A simple past question with 'did' becomes 'Was/Were + subject + past participle' in the passive.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct active form: The suspect was being questioned by the officers.
options: The officers had questioned the suspect.
The officers are questioning the suspect.
The officers were questioning the suspect.
questions.explanation: 'Was being + past participle' is the past continuous passive, so the active form is the past continuous: were questioning.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: She writes a letter to her mother every week.
options: A letter is written to her mother by her every week.
A letter was written to her mother by her every week.
A letter is being written to her mother by her every week.
A letter has been written to her mother by her every week.
questions.explanation: Present simple active becomes 'is/are + past participle' in the passive; 'was written' wrongly shifts the tense to the past.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The workers are building a dam on the Indus.
options: A dam is built on the Indus by the workers.
A dam was being built on the Indus by the workers.
A dam has been built on the Indus by the workers.
A dam is being built on the Indus by the workers.
questions.explanation: Present continuous becomes 'is/are being + past participle'; 'is built' drops 'being' and loses the continuous sense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Ali has painted the wall.
options: The wall was painted by Ali.
The wall had been painted by Ali.
The wall has painted by Ali.
The wall has been painted by Ali.
questions.explanation: Present perfect becomes 'has/have been + past participle'; 'has painted' omits 'been' and remains active in form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They had sold the house before we arrived.
options: The house had been sold before we arrived.
The house was sold before we arrived.
The house has been sold before we arrived.
The house had sold before we arrived.
questions.explanation: Past perfect becomes 'had been + past participle'; 'has been sold' wrongly changes the tense to present perfect.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The government will build new schools in rural areas.
options: New schools will be built in rural areas by the government.
New schools would be built in rural areas by the government.
New schools will have been built in rural areas by the government.
New schools will built in rural areas by the government.
questions.explanation: Future simple becomes 'will be + past participle'; 'will built' omits 'be'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They will have completed the census by June.
options: The census will be completed by June.
The census would have been completed by June.
The census will have been completed by June.
The census will have completed by June.
questions.explanation: Future perfect becomes 'will have been + past participle'; 'will be completed' loses the perfect aspect.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: You should obey the traffic rules.
options: The traffic rules should be obeyed.
The traffic rules should have been obeyed.
The traffic rules must be obeyed.
questions.explanation: Modal + verb becomes 'modal + be + past participle' with the same modal; 'must' changes the meaning of 'should'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: We can solve this problem easily.
options: This problem could be solved easily by us.
This problem can be solved easily by us.
This problem can solved easily by us.
This problem can been solved easily by us.
questions.explanation: 'Can + verb' becomes 'can be + past participle'; 'could' changes the modal and 'can been' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They may postpone the examination.
options: The examination may have been postponed.
questions.explanation: 'May + verb' becomes 'may be + past participle'; 'may have been postponed' refers to a past possibility.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The doctor ought to examine the patient.
options: The patient ought be examined by the doctor.
The patient ought to examine by the doctor.
The patient ought to have been examined by the doctor.
The patient ought to be examined by the doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Ought to + verb' becomes 'ought to be + past participle'; 'ought be' drops the necessary 'to'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Somebody has to repair the roof before the monsoon.
options: The roof has been repaired before the monsoon.
The roof has to be repaired before the monsoon.
The roof had to be repaired before the monsoon.
The roof has to repair before the monsoon.
questions.explanation: 'Has to + verb' becomes 'has to be + past participle'; 'has been repaired' changes obligation into a completed action.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Do your homework.
questions.explanation: An imperative giving an order becomes 'Let + object + be + past participle'; 'Let ... is done' uses a finite verb where the bare 'be' is required.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Please help the flood victims.
options: You were requested to help the flood victims.
You are request to help the flood victims.
You are requested to help the flood victims.
The flood victims are requested to help.
questions.explanation: A polite imperative becomes 'You are requested to + verb'; 'were requested' wrongly shifts it into the past.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Does he speak French?
questions.explanation: A present simple question with 'does' becomes 'Is/Are + subject + past participle?'; 'was' wrongly shifts the tense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Are they repairing the road?
options: Is the road repaired by them?
Is the road being repaired by them?
Was the road being repaired by them?
Has the road been repaired by them?
questions.explanation: A present continuous question becomes 'Is/Are + subject + being + past participle?'; 'Is the road repaired' drops 'being'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Has she finished the novel?
options: Had the novel been finished by her?
Is the novel finished by her?
Has the novel been finished by her?
Has the novel finished by her?
questions.explanation: A present perfect question becomes 'Has/Have + subject + been + past participle?'; 'Has the novel finished' omits 'been'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Why did the manager dismiss the clerk?
options: Why was the clerk dismissed by the manager?
Why is the clerk dismissed by the manager?
Why had the clerk been dismissed by the manager?
Why did the clerk dismissed by the manager?
questions.explanation: A past simple question with 'did' becomes 'was/were + subject + past participle'; 'did ... dismissed' wrongly keeps the auxiliary 'did'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Who invented the telephone?
options: By whom is the telephone invented?
By whom was the telephone invented?
By whom has the telephone been invented?
questions.explanation: 'Who' as subject becomes 'By whom' in the passive, and the past tense is kept with 'was invented'; 'is invented' changes the tense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Whom did you invite to the ceremony?
options: Who was invited to the ceremony by you?
Who is invited to the ceremony by you?
Whom did invited to the ceremony by you?
Who had invited to the ceremony by you?
questions.explanation: The object 'whom' becomes the subject 'who' in the passive, with 'was + past participle' for the past simple; 'is invited' changes the tense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The teacher gave him a book.
options: He is given a book by the teacher.
He was give a book by the teacher.
He was given a book by the teacher.
He has been given a book by the teacher.
questions.explanation: With two objects, the indirect object can become the subject: 'He was given a book'; 'is given' changes the tense from past to present.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They offered her a scholarship.
questions.explanation: The indirect object becomes the subject in its subject form 'she'; 'Her was offered' wrongly keeps the object pronoun.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The manager showed us the new plant.
options: The new plant is shown to us by the manager.
The new plant was showed to us by the manager.
The new plant had been shown to us by the manager.
The new plant was shown to us by the manager.
questions.explanation: When the direct object becomes the subject, the indirect object follows with 'to', and the past participle is 'shown'; 'showed' is the past simple, not the participle.

questions.prompt: The baby slept peacefully. Which statement about this sentence is correct?
options: Its passive is 'The baby was slept peacefully.'
It has no passive form because 'slept' is intransitive.
Its passive is 'Peacefully was slept by the baby.'
Its passive is 'It was slept by the baby.'
questions.explanation: Only transitive verbs, which take an object, can be put into the passive; 'sleep' has no object here, so no passive is possible.

questions.prompt: Which of the following sentences has no passive form?
questions.explanation: 'Arrive' is intransitive and takes no object, so it cannot be made passive; the other verbs all have objects that can become subjects.

questions.prompt: Prices have risen sharply this year. Which statement about this sentence is correct?
options: Its passive is 'Prices have been risen sharply this year.'
It cannot be changed into the passive because 'rise' is intransitive.
Its passive is 'Prices have been raised sharply this year.'
Its passive is 'Sharply have prices been risen this year.'
questions.explanation: 'Rise' is intransitive and has no passive; 'have been raised' uses a different, transitive verb and changes the meaning.

questions.prompt: The meeting lasted two hours. Which statement about this sentence is correct?
options: Its passive is 'Two hours were lasted by the meeting.'
It has no passive form because 'two hours' measures time and is not a true object.
Its passive is 'Two hours was lasted by the meeting.'
Its passive is 'The meeting was lasted for two hours.'
questions.explanation: Verbs of measurement such as 'last', 'cost' and 'weigh' are followed by a complement, not an object, so they cannot be made passive.

questions.prompt: Which of the following sentences cannot be put into the passive voice?
questions.explanation: 'Have' meaning possession is a stative verb that is not used in the passive; 'A new laptop is had by Sana' is unacceptable.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: People speak Pashto in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
options: Pashto is spoken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Pashto was spoken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Pashto is speaking in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Pashto has spoken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
questions.explanation: Present simple becomes 'is + past participle', and a vague agent like 'people' is usually omitted; 'is speaking' is active in form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: People believe that he is honest.
options: It is believed that he is honest.
It was believed that he is honest.
It is believed that he was honest.
It believes that he is honest.
questions.explanation: With reporting verbs, the impersonal passive 'It is believed that ...' keeps the original tenses; 'It was believed' changes the time of believing.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They say that the minister will resign.
options: It was said that the minister will resign.
It is said that the minister would resign.
It says that the minister will resign.
It is said that the minister will resign.
questions.explanation: The impersonal passive 'It is said that ...' keeps the tense of both clauses; 'It says' is active and has a different meaning.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The storm damaged many houses in Gwadar.
options: Many houses in Gwadar was damaged by the storm.
Many houses in Gwadar are damaged by the storm.
Many houses in Gwadar were damaged by the storm.
Many houses in Gwadar had damaged by the storm.
questions.explanation: Past simple becomes 'was/were + past participle', and the plural subject 'houses' needs 'were'; 'was damaged' breaks subject-verb agreement.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The committee is considering the proposal.
options: The proposal is considered by the committee.
The proposal is being considered by the committee.
The proposal was being considered by the committee.
The proposal has been considered by the committee.
questions.explanation: Present continuous becomes 'is being + past participle'; 'is considered' drops 'being' and changes the aspect.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Let him do the work.
options: Let the work be done by him.
Let the work is done by him.
The work be done by him.
Let the work done by him.
questions.explanation: 'Let + object + verb' becomes 'Let + new object + be + past participle'; 'Let the work is done' uses a finite verb after 'let'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Someone must have stolen the files.
options: The files must have been stolen.
The files must had been stolen.
questions.explanation: 'Must have + past participle' becomes 'must have been + past participle'; 'must be stolen' changes a past deduction into a present one.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They could have prevented the accident.
options: The accident could have been prevented.
The accident could had been prevented.
questions.explanation: 'Could have + past participle' becomes 'could have been + past participle'; 'could have prevented' omits 'been' and stays active.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct active form of: The thesis was being written by her.
questions.explanation: 'Was being + past participle' is the passive of the past continuous, so the active is 'was writing'; 'wrote' is past simple.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct active form of: The results will be declared by the board.
options: The board would declare the results.
The board will declare the results.
The board will be declaring the results.
questions.explanation: 'Will be + past participle' is the passive of the future simple, so the active is 'will declare'; 'would declare' changes the modal.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct active form of: Has the letter been posted by you?
questions.explanation: 'Has ... been + past participle' is the passive of the present perfect, so the active is 'Have you posted'; 'Has you' breaks agreement.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct active form of: By whom was this mosque built?
questions.explanation: 'By whom' becomes the subject 'who', and 'was built' (past simple passive) becomes 'built'; 'whom' cannot be a subject.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Allama Iqbal wrote Bang-e-Dra.
options: Bang-e-Dra is written by Allama Iqbal.
Bang-e-Dra was written by Allama Iqbal.
Bang-e-Dra was wrote by Allama Iqbal.
Bang-e-Dra had been written by Allama Iqbal.
questions.explanation: Past simple becomes 'was + past participle', and the participle of 'write' is 'written'; 'was wrote' wrongly uses the past simple form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The Prime Minister is going to inaugurate the motorway.
options: The motorway will be inaugurated by the Prime Minister.
The motorway is going to inaugurated by the Prime Minister.
The motorway is going to be inaugurated by the Prime Minister.
The motorway was going to be inaugurated by the Prime Minister.
questions.explanation: 'Is going to + verb' becomes 'is going to be + past participle'; 'will be inaugurated' changes the form rather than converting it.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Farmers used to grow cotton here.
options: Cotton used to be grown here.
Cotton was used to be grown here.
Cotton is used to grow here.
questions.explanation: 'Used to + verb' becomes 'used to be + past participle'; 'was used to be' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Somebody is following us.
questions.explanation: Present continuous becomes 'am/is/are being + past participle', and the object 'us' becomes the subject 'we'; 'Us are' keeps the object form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The public must not tolerate corruption.
options: Corruption must not tolerated by the public.
Corruption must not have been tolerated by the public.
Corruption must not be tolerated by the public.
Corruption need not be tolerated by the public.
questions.explanation: 'Must not + verb' becomes 'must not be + past participle'; 'need not' changes a prohibition into a lack of necessity.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They made him sign the paper.
options: He was made sign the paper.
He made to sign the paper.
He was made to sign the paper.
He was making to sign the paper.
questions.explanation: After 'make' in the passive, the bare infinitive becomes a to-infinitive: 'was made to sign'; 'was made sign' omits 'to'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Nobody has answered my question.
options: My question has not been answered.
My question had not been answered.
questions.explanation: 'Nobody' becomes a negative passive with the tense kept: 'has not been answered'; 'was not answered' changes the present perfect to the past simple.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: They elected him chairman of the board.
options: He is elected chairman of the board.
Chairman of the board was elected him.
He was elect chairman of the board.
He was elected chairman of the board.
questions.explanation: The object 'him' becomes the subject 'he', and the complement 'chairman' stays after the verb; 'is elected' changes the tense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: We should take care of the elderly.
options: The elderly should be taken care.
The elderly should take care of.
The elderly should be taken care of.
The elderly should have been taken care of.
questions.explanation: With prepositional verbs, the preposition stays after the participle: 'taken care of'; dropping 'of' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Everyone laughed at the joke.
options: The joke was laughed by everyone.
The joke is laughed at by everyone.
The joke was laughed at by everyone.
The joke laughed at by everyone.
questions.explanation: 'Laugh at' is a prepositional verb, so 'at' must be kept in the passive; 'was laughed by everyone' drops it.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The nurse looks after the patients.
options: The patients is looked after by the nurse.
The patients are looked by the nurse.
The patients were looked after by the nurse.
The patients are looked after by the nurse.
questions.explanation: Present simple becomes 'are + past participle' for a plural subject, and the particle 'after' is kept; 'are looked by' drops it.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: Who is teaching you English?
options: By whom are you taught English?
Who are you being taught English?
By whom were you being taught English?
By whom are you being taught English?
questions.explanation: Present continuous with 'who' becomes 'By whom ... being + past participle'; 'are you taught' loses the continuous aspect.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form of: The flood has swept away the bridge.
options: The bridge has swept away by the flood.
The bridge has been swept away by the flood.
The bridge was swept away by the flood.
The bridge has been swept by the flood away.
questions.explanation: Present perfect becomes 'has been + past participle', and the particle 'away' stays with the verb; 'was swept' changes the tense.

topics.title: Direct and Indirect Speech
topics.summary: Reporting what someone said, asked or ordered, with the correct changes to tense, pronouns, word order and time words.

rules.rule: When the reporting verb is in the past, move the tenses one step back: am/is → was, have → had, past → past perfect, will → would, can → could.
examples: He said, "I am busy." → He said that he was busy.
She said, "I will come." → She said that she would come.

rules.rule: Do not change the tense if the reporting verb is in the present, or if the statement is a universal truth.
examples: He says, "I am busy." → He says that he is busy.
The teacher said that light travels faster than sound.

rules.rule: Change pronouns to fit the new speaker, and change words of time and place: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, here → there, this → that.
examples: She said, "I met him yesterday." → She said that she had met him the previous day.
He said, "I live here." → He said that he lived there.

rules.rule: Report yes/no questions with if or whether, and wh-questions with the question word. Use statement word order and no question mark.
examples: He asked, "Are you ready?" → He asked whether I was ready.
She asked, "Why are you late?" → She asked why I was late.

rules.rule: Report commands and requests with told, ordered, requested or advised + object + to-infinitive; for negatives, use 'not to'.
examples: He said to me, "Sit down." → He told me to sit down.
She said to them, "Don't shout." → She told them not to shout.

rules.rule: 'Said to + person' becomes 'told + person'; 'said' is not followed directly by a person as object.
examples: He told me that he was leaving.
He said that he was leaving.

rules.rule: Exclamations are reported with verbs such as exclaimed, and are turned into statements.
examples: She said, "How lovely the view is!" → She exclaimed that the view was very lovely.
He said, "Alas! I have lost." → He exclaimed sadly that he had lost.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: She said, "I am waiting for the bus."
options: She said that she was waiting for the bus.
She said that I was waiting for the bus.
She told that she was waiting for the bus.
She said that she had been waited for the bus.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'am waiting' becomes 'was waiting' and 'I' becomes 'she'; 'told' needs a person as object.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said to me, "I will help you tomorrow."
options: He said me that he would help me the next day.
He told me that he would help me the next day.
He told me that I would help him the next day.
He told me that he will help you tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Said to me' becomes 'told me', 'will' becomes 'would', pronouns change, and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."
options: The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
The teacher told that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth will revolve around the sun.
questions.explanation: A universal truth keeps its present tense in indirect speech; 'told' would need a person as object.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: She asked me, "Where do you live?"
options: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where do you live.
She asked me that where I lived.
She asked me where I lived.
questions.explanation: A reported wh-question uses statement word order (I lived), drops 'do/did', and does not add 'that'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: He asked, "Have you finished the report?"
options: He asked whether I had finished the report.
He asked that had I finished the report.
He asked whether had I finished the report.
He asked me have you finished the report?
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether' or 'if', in statement word order, with the tense moved back (have → had).

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: The officer said to the guard, "Open the gate."
options: The officer told the guard that open the gate.
The officer ordered the guard to open the gate.
The officer ordered the guard opening the gate.
The officer said the guard to open the gate.
questions.explanation: A command is reported with a verb such as 'ordered' + object + to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: Mother said to me, "Do not play in the sun."
options: Mother told me to not playing in the sun.
Mother told me don't play in the sun.
Mother told me not to play in the sun.
Mother told me that do not play in the sun.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported with 'told + object + not to + base verb'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said, "I met her yesterday."
options: He said that he had meet her the previous day.
He said that he has met her the day before.
He said that I had met her the previous day.
He said that he had met her the previous day.
questions.explanation: The simple past becomes the past perfect (had met) and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: She said, "What a beautiful garden this is!"
options: She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful garden.
She exclaimed what a beautiful garden is this.
She said that what a beautiful garden this was!
She exclaimed that what a beautiful garden it is.
questions.explanation: An exclamation is reported with 'exclaimed' and turned into an ordinary statement with the tense moved back and no exclamation mark.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: He said, "I can solve this problem."
options: He said that he can solved this problem.
He said that he could solve that problem.
He said that I could solve that problem.
He said that he could solved that problem.
questions.explanation: 'Can' becomes 'could' (followed by the base verb), 'I' becomes 'he', and 'this' becomes 'that'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: Ayesha said, "I have been working here for five years."
options: Ayesha said that she was been working there for five years.
Ayesha said that I had been working there for five years.
Ayesha said that she had been working there for five years.
Ayesha said that she had been worked there for five years.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous becomes the past perfect continuous (had been working), and 'here' becomes 'there'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech: Bilal said to the principal, "Sir, please grant me leave."
options: Bilal said the principal please grant me leave.
Bilal respectfully told the principal that grant him leave.
Bilal requested the principal grant me leave.
Bilal respectfully requested the principal to grant him leave.
questions.explanation: A polite request is reported with 'requested + object + to-infinitive'; 'Sir' is replaced by 'respectfully', and 'me' becomes 'him'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I am writing a novel."
options: He said that I was writing a novel.
He said that he had been writing a novel.
He said that he was writing a novel.
He said that he was write a novel.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, the present continuous shifts to the past continuous and 'I' becomes 'he'; 'had been writing' is the wrong back-shift.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I bought this dress last week."
options: She said that she had bought that dress the previous week.
She said that she had bought this dress last week.
She said that she has bought that dress the previous week.
She said that I had bought that dress the previous week.
questions.explanation: The past simple shifts to the past perfect, 'this' becomes 'that' and 'last week' becomes 'the previous week'; keeping 'this ... last week' ignores the time and place changes.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to me, "You are late."
options: He told me that you were late.
He said me that I was late.
He told me that I was late.
He told to me that I was late.
questions.explanation: 'Said to' becomes 'told', 'you' becomes 'I' to match the listener, and 'are' becomes 'was'; 'said me' is ungrammatical because 'say' needs 'to' before a person.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: The teacher said, "Honesty is the best policy."
options: The teacher said that honesty is the best policy.
The teacher said that honesty was the best policy.
The teacher said that honesty had been the best policy.
The teacher said that honesty would be the best policy.
questions.explanation: A universal truth or proverb keeps its present tense in indirect speech; changing it to 'was' wrongly makes it time-bound.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I will go to Karachi tomorrow."
options: She said that she would go to Karachi the next day.
She said that she will go to Karachi tomorrow.
She said that she would go to Karachi tomorrow.
She said that she will go to Karachi the next day.
questions.explanation: 'Will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'; 'would go ... tomorrow' changes the verb but not the time word.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I may come late."
options: He said that he may come late.
He said that he might come late.
He said that he must come late.
He said that he would come late.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'may' becomes 'might'; 'would' changes the meaning from possibility to certainty.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I must leave now."
options: She said that she has to leave now.
She said that she had to leave now.
She said that she would leave then.
She said that she had to leave then.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expressing present obligation becomes 'had to', and 'now' becomes 'then'; 'had to leave now' fails to change the time word.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I was ill yesterday."
options: He said that he was ill yesterday.
He said that he has been ill the day before.
He said that he had been ill yesterday.
He said that he had been ill the day before.
questions.explanation: The past simple 'was' shifts to 'had been', and 'yesterday' becomes 'the day before' or 'the previous day'; keeping 'yesterday' ignores the time shift.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I have finished my work."
options: She said that she has finished her work.
She said that she had finished her work.
She said that she had finished my work.
She said that she had finish her work.
questions.explanation: The present perfect shifts to the past perfect and 'my' becomes 'her'; 'had finished my work' leaves the possessive unchanged.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to me, "Are you coming with us?"
options: He asked me if I am coming with them.
He asked me whether was I coming with them.
He asked me if I was coming with them.
He asked me if I was coming with us.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether' in statement word order, with back-shift and pronoun changes; 'whether was I' keeps the question order.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said to him, "Why are you crying?"
options: She asked him why he was crying.
She asked him why was he crying.
She asked him why he is crying.
She asked him that why he was crying.
questions.explanation: A wh-question is reported with the question word and normal statement order, without 'that'; 'why was he crying' keeps the inverted question order.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: The officer said, "Who has signed this letter?"
options: The officer asked who has signed this letter.
The officer asked who had signed this letter.
The officer asked that who had signed that letter.
The officer asked who had signed that letter.
questions.explanation: The present perfect shifts to the past perfect and 'this' becomes 'that', while 'said' becomes 'asked'; adding 'that' before 'who' is wrong.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to me, "How old are you?"
options: He asked me how old was I.
He asked me how old I was.
He asked me how old I am.
He asked me how old you were.
questions.explanation: In reported questions the subject comes before the verb: 'how old I was'; 'how old was I' keeps the direct question order.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said to me, "Did you see the film?"
options: She asked me whether I had seen the film.
She asked me whether had I seen the film.
She asked me that whether I had seen the film.
She asked me whether I have seen the film.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary 'did' is dropped, the past simple shifts to the past perfect and the order becomes subject + verb; 'whether had I seen' keeps the question order.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: The teacher said to the students, "Sit down."
options: The teacher ordered the students that sit down.
The teacher said the students to sit down.
The teacher ordered the students sit down.
The teacher ordered the students to sit down.
questions.explanation: A command is reported with a verb such as 'ordered' or 'told' followed by the to-infinitive; 'ordered ... that sit down' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to his servant, "Bring me a glass of water."
options: He ordered his servant to bring me a glass of water.
He ordered his servant that bring him a glass of water.
He ordered his servant bring him a glass of water.
He ordered his servant to bring him a glass of water.
questions.explanation: A command becomes 'ordered + object + to-infinitive', and 'me' (the speaker) becomes 'him'; keeping 'me' refers to the wrong person.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said to me, "Please lend me your pen."
options: She requested me to lend her my pen.
She requested me to lend me your pen.
She requested me that lend her my pen.
She said me to lend her my pen.
questions.explanation: A request with 'please' is reported with 'requested' + to-infinitive, and pronouns change to fit the reporter; 'lend me your pen' leaves the pronouns unchanged.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to them, "Do not make a noise."
options: He told them do not make a noise.
He told them that don't make a noise.
He told them not to make a noise.
He told them not make a noise.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported as 'not to + verb'; 'not make' omits the necessary 'to'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "Alas! I have lost my purse."
options: He exclaimed with joy that he had lost his purse.
He said alas that he had lost his purse.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he has lost my purse.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his purse.
questions.explanation: 'Alas' expresses sorrow, so the exclamation is reported with 'exclaimed with sorrow', the present perfect shifts back and 'my' becomes 'his'; 'with joy' contradicts 'alas'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "Hurrah! We have won the match."
options: She exclaimed with sorrow that they had won the match.
She exclaimed with joy that we had won the match.
She exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
She exclaimed with joy that they have won the match.
questions.explanation: 'Hurrah' expresses joy; 'we' becomes 'they' and 'have won' becomes 'had won'; keeping 'we' does not fit the reporter's point of view.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "What a fool I am!"
options: He exclaimed that he was a great fool.
He exclaimed that what a fool he was.
He exclaimed that he is a great fool.
He exclaimed that I was a great fool.
questions.explanation: An exclamation with 'what' is reported as a statement with an intensifier such as 'great', with tense and pronoun changes; 'that what a fool' wrongly combines 'that' with the exclamatory form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said to me, "May you succeed in the examination!"
options: She prayed that you might succeed in the examination.
She said me that I might succeed in the examination.
She prayed that I might succeed in the examination.
She prayed that may I succeed in the examination.
questions.explanation: A wish or prayer with 'may' is reported with 'prayed' or 'wished', and 'may' becomes 'might'; 'that may I succeed' keeps the inverted wish order.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: The student said to the principal, "Good morning, sir."
options: The student respectfully said the principal good morning.
The student respectfully wished the principal good morning.
The student told the principal that good morning sir.
The student wished good morning to sir.
questions.explanation: Greetings are reported with 'wished', and 'sir' is shown by 'respectfully'; 'said the principal good morning' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to his friends, "Let's go for a walk."
options: He proposed to his friends to let them go for a walk.
He told his friends let's go for a walk.
He proposed his friends that we should go for a walk.
He proposed to his friends that they should go for a walk.
questions.explanation: 'Let's' expressing a suggestion is reported with 'proposed' or 'suggested' + 'that ... should'; 'to let them go' changes the suggestion into a request for permission.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "Let me finish my sentence."
options: She proposed that they should finish her sentence.
She asked to be allowed to finish her sentence.
She asked to be allowed to finish my sentence.
She suggested to let me finish my sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Let me' asking for permission is reported as 'asked to be allowed to'; 'proposed that they should' wrongly treats it as a suggestion.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I will be travelling next week."
options: She said that she would be travelling the following week.
She said that she will be travelling next week.
She said that she would be travelling next week.
She said that she would travelled the following week.
questions.explanation: 'Will be' becomes 'would be' and 'next week' becomes 'the following week'; 'would be travelling next week' leaves the time word unchanged.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I will have finished the report by noon."
options: He said that he will have finished the report by noon.
He said that he would has finished the report by noon.
He said that he had finished the report by noon.
He said that he would have finished the report by noon.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: The teacher said, "Two and two make four."
options: The teacher said that two and two made four.
The teacher said that two and two had made four.
The teacher said that two and two would make four.
The teacher said that two and two make four.
questions.explanation: A mathematical fact is a universal truth, so its tense is not changed; 'made' wrongly back-shifts it.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I go for a walk every morning."
options: She said that she had went for a walk every morning.
She said that she was go for a walk every morning.
She said that she went for a walk every morning.
She said that I went for a walk every morning.
questions.explanation: A present simple habit shifts to the past simple after 'said', and 'I' becomes 'she'; 'had went' is ungrammatical.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I live here."
options: He said that he lived here.
He said that he had lived there.
He said that I lived there.
He said that he lived there.
questions.explanation: The present simple shifts to the past simple and 'here' becomes 'there'; keeping 'here' ignores the change of place.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: She said, "I met him two days ago."
options: She said that she met him two days ago.
She said that she had met him two days before.
She said that she had met him two days ago.
She said that she has met him two days before.
questions.explanation: The past simple shifts to the past perfect and 'ago' becomes 'before'; 'had met him two days ago' leaves the time word unchanged.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, "I am leaving this evening."
options: He said that he was leaving this evening.
He said that he is leaving that evening.
He said that he was leaving that evening.
He said that he had leaving that evening.
questions.explanation: The present continuous becomes the past continuous and 'this evening' becomes 'that evening'; keeping 'this evening' ignores the time shift.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said to me, "Can you drive a truck?"
options: He asked me if I can drive a truck.
He asked me if I could drive a truck.
He asked me could I drive a truck.
He asked me if you could drive a truck.
